title: Serving a Model as a Service
intro: A trained model only creates value once other systems can call it. Here's the path from a saved model directory to a load-balanced service on Kubernetes.

steps.prompt: Serve a saved TensorFlow model locally with TensorFlow Serving, mounting ./model into the container.
steps.fake_output:
I tensorflow_serving/model_servers/server.cc:430] Running gRPC ModelServer at 0.0.0.0:8500
I ...server.cc:450] Exporting HTTP/REST API at:localhost:8501
steps.explanation: The model is served over REST on 8501 (and gRPC on 8500).
steps.why: Dedicated model servers (TF Serving, TorchServe, Triton) handle batching, versioning, and GPU scheduling for you. Wrapping a model in a hand-written Flask app works, but you end up reimplementing those features badly.

steps.explanation: The model returns a score for the one input instance.
steps.why: Keep a few known input/output pairs and check them after every deployment. A model that loads and responds can still return garbage — only a known-answer test catches that.

steps.prompt: Check which model versions the server has loaded.
steps.why: TF Serving watches numbered subdirectories (model/1, model/2, model/3) and serves the latest. Keeping old versions on disk means rollback is just removing the newest directory.

steps.prompt: Deploy the model server to Kubernetes from its manifest.
steps.explanation: The same container, now as a managed, self-healing Deployment.
steps.why: Give model servers a readiness probe that only passes once the model has finished loading — large models can take minutes, and sending traffic before then causes errors on every new pod.

steps.prompt: Expose it inside the cluster on port 8501.
steps.explanation: Other services can now call http://model-server:8501.
steps.why: From here, the model is just another service — it gets the same scaling, monitoring, and rollout tooling as everything else. That's the core idea of MLOps.
